# Attest

> Type assertions and benchmarks

# Getting started

> Install attest and run its setup and teardown around your tests.

Attest is a testing library that makes your TypeScript types available at runtime. A test can assert on a value's type, the type errors and completions of an expression, and the type instantiations a block costs, next to ordinary value assertions. Assertions work from Vitest, Mocha, Jest or any runner with global setup and teardown hooks.

Benches run as plain scripts. They report how many type instantiations a block contributes, which is deterministic for a given TypeScript version, and how long a call takes.

ArkType uses attest to check that its runtime parser and its types agree, and to keep its editor performance from regressing.

## Installation

```bash
npm install -D @ark/attest
```

> **Note**
>
> attest is still in alpha, so its API can change between minor versions. Your feedback will help us iterate toward a stable 1.0.

If you're upgrading, [Upgrading](https://arktype.io/docs/upgrading#attest) lists the changes to benches.

## Global setup

Type assertions need `setup` to run once before your tests and `teardown` once after them.

`setup` type-checks your project once and writes what each `attest` call needs, like its argument's type and the type errors in it, to `.attest/assertions.json`. Assertions read that file rather than starting TypeScript in every test worker. `teardown` (also exported as `cleanup`) writes the snapshots your tests populated or updated back into your source files when the run exits.

Add `.attest` to your `.gitignore`.

### Vitest

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config"

export default defineConfig({
	test: {
		globalSetup: ["setupVitest.ts"]
	}
})
```

```ts
import { setup } from "@ark/attest"

// setup returns teardown, which Vitest calls after the last test
export default () => setup({})
```

Vitest rejects command-line flags it doesn't know, so pass attest [options](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/options) to it as `ATTEST_` environment variables. Its own `-u` flag works, and updates attest's snapshots along with Vitest's.

### Mocha

```json
"mocha": {
	"require": "./setupMocha.ts"
}
```

```ts
import { setup, teardown } from "@ark/attest"

export const mochaGlobalSetup = () => setup({})

export const mochaGlobalTeardown = teardown
```

### Jest

```js
export default {
	globalSetup: "./setupJest.ts",
	globalTeardown: "./teardownJest.ts"
}
```

```ts
import { setup } from "@ark/attest"

export default () => setup({})
```

```ts
import { teardown } from "@ark/attest"

export default teardown
```

`@ark/attest` is an ES module, so Jest has to run with ES module support, e.g. ts-jest with `useESM` and `NODE_OPTIONS=--experimental-vm-modules`.

### Bun

```ts
import { setup } from "@ark/attest"

setup({})
```

```bash
bun test --preload ./setupBun.ts
```

You can also list the file under `preload` in the `[test]` section of `bunfig.toml`.

Under `bun test`, assertions compare against existing snapshots, but new or updated snapshots aren't written: attest writes them when the process exits, and `bun test` doesn't emit Node's `exit` event.

## Iterating quickly

Type-checking the project is the slow part of `setup`. Two options cut it down:

- [`skipTypes`](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/options#skiptypes) skips the check along with every type assertion, for when you're only changing runtime code.
- [`onlyNamedTestFiles`](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/options#onlynamedtestfiles) checks only the test files you name on the command line.

## TypeScript versions

Attest analyzes your project with whichever `typescript` it resolves, which is normally your own install since it's a peer dependency. To test several versions, run your suite once per version, e.g. in a CI matrix that installs each one.

TypeScript 7.1+ is supported through its native API. 7.0.x throws an error asking you to upgrade. Under TypeScript 7:

- Instantiation counts come from running `tsc --extendedDiagnostics --singleThreaded` per bench. `tsc` fully checks a bench's dependencies before measuring it, so work the bench shares with them isn't counted, and counts can run lower than on TypeScript 5 or 6. Re-record bench baselines when you switch.
- Type strings, union ordering and error elaboration can differ, so some snapshots need updating when you switch.
- Benches write temporary `.attest-*` copies beside their source files while measuring, so the source directory has to be writable.

# Assertions

> Assert on types, values, errors, completions, JSDoc and type instantiations from any test runner.

Assertions work from any test runner once [setup](https://arktype.io/docs/attest#global-setup) has run.

## Types

```ts
import { attest } from "@ark/attest"
import { type } from "arktype"

const Even = type("number%2")

// passes if Even.infer and number are assignable to each other
attest<number>(Even.infer)
// compares two types without a value
attest<number, typeof Even.infer>()
// snapshots the type as TypeScript displays it
attest(Even.infer).type.toString.snap("number")
```

`.type.errors` checks the type errors TypeScript reports for the expression passed to `attest`:

```ts
import { attest } from "@ark/attest"
import { type } from "arktype"

// @ts-expect-error
attest(() => type({ "[object]": "string" })).type.errors(
	"Indexed key definition 'object' must be a string or symbol"
)
```

> **Strings match as substrings**
>
> `.type.toString`, `.type.errors`, `.throws` and `.jsdoc` pass if the string you give appears anywhere in the actual one, so `attest([1]).type.toString("number")` passes although the type is `number[]`. They also accept a `RegExp`. Chain `.snap` for an exact match.

## Values

```ts
import { attest } from "@ark/attest"

const user = { name: "Alan Turing", born: 1912 }

// deep equality
attest(user).equals({ name: "Alan Turing", born: 1912 })
// Object.is equality
attest(user.born).is(1912)
// validates the value against an ArkType definition
attest(user).satisfies({ name: "string", born: "number.integer" })
attest(new Date(0)).instanceOf(Date)
// written into the call on the first run, compared after that
attest(user).snap({ name: "Alan Turing", born: 1912 })
```

The expected value of `.equals`, `.is` and `.snap` has to match the type of the value under test. Chain `.unknown` first, as in `attest(user).unknown.equals(...)`, to compare against anything.

`.unwrap()` returns what an assertion would compare rather than asserting on it, e.g. `attest(user).type.toString.unwrap()` returns `"{ name: string; born: number }"`.

## Errors

`.throws` calls the function passed to `attest` and checks what it threw. The thrown value is converted with `String()`, so it starts with the error's name.

```ts
import { attest } from "@ark/attest"

const divide = (a: number, b: number) => {
	if (b === 0) throw new RangeError("Cannot divide by zero")
	return a / b
}

attest(() => divide(1, 0)).throws("divide by zero")
attest(() => divide(1, 0)).throws(/^RangeError/)
attest(() => divide(1, 0)).throws.snap("RangeError: Cannot divide by zero")
```

Chain `.type.errors` to check the type error of the same call:

```ts
import { attest } from "@ark/attest"

const assertFalse = (value: false) => {
	if (value) throw new Error(`${value} is not false`)
}

// @ts-expect-error
attest(() => assertFalse(true))
	.throws("true is not false")
	.type.errors("Argument of type 'true' is not assignable")
```

When the runtime error and the type error share a message, `throwsAndHasTypeError` checks both:

```ts
import { attest } from "@ark/attest"
import { type } from "arktype"

// @ts-expect-error
attest(() => type("number%0")).throwsAndHasTypeError(
	"% operator must be followed by a non-zero integer literal (was 0)"
)
```

## Completions

`.completions` snapshots the completions TypeScript offers for each string literal in the expression passed to `attest`. A partial literal is usually a type error, and if it would also throw at runtime, wrap it in a function:

```ts
import { attest } from "@ark/attest"
import { type } from "arktype"

// @ts-expect-error
attest(() => type({ b: "b" })).completions({ b: ["bigint", "boolean"] })
```

Quoted keys get completions too. Prettier removes quotes it doesn't need, which would leave nothing to complete, so keep it from formatting the line:

```ts
import { attest } from "@ark/attest"

type Legends = { faker?: "🐐"; [others: string]: unknown }

// prettier-ignore
attest({ "f": "🐐" } as Legends).completions({ f: ["faker"] })
```

Completions are keyed by the literal's text, so two identical literals in one `attest` call throw "Encountered multiple completion candidates". Split them into separate calls.

## JSDoc

`.jsdoc` reads the JSDoc of the value passed to `attest` when it's a variable or a property access:

```ts
import { attest } from "@ark/attest"
import { type } from "arktype"

const T = type({
	/** FOO */
	foo: "string"
})

const out = T.assert({ foo: "foo" })

attest(out.foo).jsdoc.snap("FOO")
```

## Conditional assertions

Assertions are ordinary function calls, so runtime logic can decide which ones run:

```ts
import { attest } from "@ark/attest"
import ts from "typescript"

const value = Math.random() > 0.5 ? "a" : 1

// TypeScript 7 orders this union differently
if (Number.parseInt(ts.version) >= 7)
	attest(value).type.toString.snap('"a" | 1')
else attest(value).type.toString.snap('1 | "a"')
```

## Instantiations

`attest.instantiations` snapshots the number of type instantiations contributed by the test that calls it, counted like a [bench](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/benches#type-benches) counts its block:

```ts
import { attest } from "@ark/attest"
import { type } from "arktype"

it("discriminated union", () => {
	const User = type({
		kind: "'admin'",
		"powers?": "string[]"
	})
		.or({
			kind: "'superadmin'",
			"superpowers?": "string[]"
		})
		.or({
			kind: "'pleb'"
		})

	// measured with TypeScript 6.0.3
	attest.instantiations([17010, "instantiations"])
})
```

Unlike a bench, it throws inside the test when the count exceeds its baseline by more than [`benchPercentThreshold`](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/options). Counts differ between TypeScript versions, so record them with the version you test against.

## Snapshots

A `.snap()` or `.completions()` with no argument is populated on the first run: [teardown](https://arktype.io/docs/attest#global-setup) writes the value into the call in your source file, then formats the file with [`formatCmd`](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/options), Prettier by default.

To rewrite every snapshot with the current values, pass `--updateSnapshots` to your test command or set `ATTEST_updateSnapshots=true`. `-u` and `--update` work too, unless your runner claims them: Mocha's `-u` is its `--ui` flag.

If a `CI` environment variable is set, a snapshot with no value throws rather than being populated, so a test can't pass in CI without its expected value. Set [`failOnMissingSnapshots`](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/options) to change that.

`.snap.toFile(name)` stores the snapshot in `assert.snapshots.json` beside the test file rather than inline, keyed by the test file's name and then `name`. Pass `{ path }` to use another file, relative to the test's directory or absolute.

```ts
import { attest } from "@ark/attest"

attest({ name: "Alan Turing" }).snap.toFile("user")
```

## contextualize

`contextualize` wraps a test file's tests in a `describe` named after the file, e.g. `divisor` for `__tests__/divisor.test.ts`. It needs global `describe` and `it` functions, as in Mocha, or Vitest with `globals: true`.

```ts
import { attest, contextualize } from "@ark/attest"

contextualize(() => {
	it("adds", () => {
		attest(1 + 1).equals(2)
	})
})
```

Pass a function before the tests to create a fresh context for each one:

```ts
import { attest, contextualize } from "@ark/attest"

contextualize(
	() => new Map<string, number>(),
	it => {
		it("starts empty", map => {
			attest(map.size).equals(0)
		})
	}
)
```

`contextualize.each(name, createContext, tests)` does the same for a named `describe` within the file.

# Benches

> Measure the type instantiations and runtime of a block of code against a baseline stored inline.

A bench file is a plain script that needs no `setup`. Run it with `node benches.ts`, which strips the types on Node 22.18+, or any TypeScript runner. The first run writes each result into its call as the baseline, and later runs compare against it.

## Type benches

`.types()` counts the type instantiations of checking a bench's function and of evaluating the type it returns as fully as displaying it would. TypeScript defers the members of types like mapped types until something reads them, so return the result you want measured.

```ts
import { bench } from "@ark/attest"

// combinatorial template literals are often expensive
type makeComplexType<s extends string> =
	s extends `${infer head}${infer tail}` ? head | tail | makeComplexType<tail>
	:	s

bench("short string", () => {
	return {} as makeComplexType<"defenestration">
}).types([163, "instantiations"])

// about twice the count for twice the length, so the type is O(n)
bench("long string", () => {
	return {} as makeComplexType<"antidisestablishmentarianism">
}).types([317, "instantiations"])
```

A count is deterministic for a given TypeScript version and code. These were measured with TypeScript 6.0.3.

## Baseline expressions

A bench's count is what its block adds to checking the rest of the file with every bench removed. The first call to an API instantiates types that later calls reuse, so without a baseline, each bench pays for that work. Put it in `bench.baseline`, which does nothing at runtime but stays in the file attest checks.

```ts
import { bench } from "@ark/attest"
import { type } from "arktype"

bench.baseline(() => type("never"))

bench("single-quoted", () => type("'nineteen characters'")).types([
	731,
	"instantiations"
])

bench("keyword", () => type("string")).types([511, "instantiations"])
```

On TypeScript 6.0.3, these benches count 13484 and 13408 without the baseline.

> **Warning**
>
> Don't bench an expression identical to your baseline expression. The bench would reuse the baseline's cached types and count fewer instantiations, or none.

## Runtime benches

`.median()` records the median time of a call, picking `ns`, `us`, `ms` or `s` on the first run.

```ts
import { bench } from "@ark/attest"
import { type } from "arktype"

// an export, so V8 can't treat the input as a constant
export const data = { name: "Alan Turing", age: 41 }

const User = type({ name: "string", age: "number.integer" })

// the first run writes a result like [4.22, "ns"]
bench("validate user", () => User(data)).median()
```

To measure what you mean to:

- Return the result the bench computes. Each bench runs in a loop compiled for it alone, so V8 can inline it and drop any work whose result is unused. attest warns if a bench returns `undefined`.
- Read inputs from an export rather than a literal or a local `const`, so V8 can't fold work on constant inputs. This matters most for small functions like a primitive check.
- Prefer `.median()`, which is robust to the GC pauses and preemption that skew `.mean()`. `.mark()` records both.
- Benches in a process share the code of the library they call, so a bench can read faster or slower depending on which benches ran before it. Only compare results between runs of the same file in the same order.

Timings depend on the machine, so treat a runtime baseline as specific to the machine that recorded it.

A runtime assertion can chain `.types()` to check the same bench's instantiations, as in `bench(...).median().types()`.

### Options

```ts
import { bench } from "@ark/attest"

export const items: number[] = []

bench("push", () => items.push(1), {
	// stop sampling after 1 second or 10,000 samples, whichever comes first
	until: { ms: 1000, count: 10_000 },
	// runs outside the timed section, after each sample
	hooks: { afterCall: () => (items.length = 0) }
}).median()
```

After a warmup of 500ms (or `until.ms`, if shorter), attest samples for 5 seconds or 100,000 samples, whichever comes first. A sample times as many calls as fit in about 0.2ms, so `hooks` run once per sample, not once per call.

### Async benches

A bench that returns a promise is awaited on every call, and its runtime assertion returns a promise:

```ts
import { bench } from "@ark/attest"

export const bytes = new TextEncoder().encode("Alan Turing")

await bench("sha-256", () => crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", bytes)).median()
```

## Running one bench

`--filter` runs only the bench with that exact name:

```bash
node benches.ts --filter keyword
```

## Updating baselines

Pass `--updateSnapshots` (or `-u`) to rewrite every baseline in the file with the new results. A result more than `benchPercentThreshold` under its baseline prints 📉 as a reminder to record a new one.

## Thresholds

A result fails if it exceeds its baseline by more than `benchPercentThreshold` (20% by default). The bench prints 📈 when it runs, and the file prints ❌ for each failure when it exits, with exit code 1. [`attest.instantiations`](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/assertions#instantiations) throws inside its test instead.

`benchErrorOnThresholdExceeded` decides which results fail. It's `true` (all) by default and can be `false`, `"types"` or `"runtime"`. Timings vary between runs and counts don't, so to fail only type benches:

```bash
node benches.ts --benchErrorOnThresholdExceeded types --benchPercentThreshold 10
```

# Options

> Every attest option, its default, and how to set it from setup, a flag or an environment variable.

Set an option in one of three ways:

- Pass it to `setup`, e.g. `setup({ skipTypes: true })`.
- Pass it as a flag to the process that runs your tests or benches, e.g. `--skipTypes` or `--benchPercentThreshold 10`. A boolean option is turned on by its flag alone.
- Set it as an environment variable prefixed with `ATTEST_`, e.g. `ATTEST_skipTypes=true` or `ATTEST_benchPercentThreshold=10`. Values are parsed as JSON, so a string needs quotes: `ATTEST_filter='"keyword"'`.

Flags and options passed to `setup` both override environment variables. Avoid setting an option both in `setup` and as a flag: `setup` uses its own value, but your tests use the flag's. Benches don't call `setup`, so they read only flags and environment variables.

## Options

| Option | Default | Effect |
| - | - | - |
| `skipTypes` | `false` | Skip type-checking in `setup` and every type assertion. See [below](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/options#skiptypes). |
| `onlyNamedTestFiles` | `false` | Type-check only the test files named on the command line. See [below](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/options#onlynamedtestfiles). |
| `checker` | see [below](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/options#checker) | The type checker to analyze with: `"tsjs"`, `"tsgo"` or `"tsrs"`. |
| `updateSnapshots` | `false` | Rewrite every snapshot and bench baseline with the current value. Also `-u` or `--update`. |
| `failOnMissingSnapshots` | `true` if `CI` is set | Throw on a `.snap()` with no value rather than populating it. |
| `tsconfig` | nearest `tsconfig.json` | Path of the tsconfig to analyze. By default, attest looks in the working directory, then its parents. `null` ignores tsconfig files and uses only `compilerOptions`. |
| `compilerOptions` | `{}` | Compiler options, as written in a tsconfig, merged over the tsconfig's. As a flag, pass JSON. |
| `attestAliases` | `["attest", "attestInternal"]` | Names of the functions whose calls `setup` analyzes. Replaces the default. As a flag, separate names with commas. See [Custom assertions](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/integration). |
| `skipInlineInstantiations` | `false` | Skip measuring and checking [`attest.instantiations`](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/assertions#instantiations). |
| `testDeclarationAliases` | `["bench", "it", "test"]` | Names of the calls whose blocks count as a bench or test when counting instantiations. |
| `benchPercentThreshold` | `20` | How far a result can exceed its baseline, in percent, before it fails. See [Thresholds](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/benches#thresholds). |
| `benchErrorOnThresholdExceeded` | `true` | Which results over the threshold fail: `true` (all), `false`, `"types"` or `"runtime"`. |
| `filter` | none | Run only the bench with this name. |
| `formatCmd` | `npm exec --no -- prettier --write` | Command run on each file attest writes snapshots into. |
| `shouldFormat` | `true` | Whether to run `formatCmd`. |
| `typeToStringFormat` | `{}` | Prettier options for type strings. See [below](https://arktype.io/docs/attest/options#typetostringformat). |

`getDefaultAttestConfig()` returns the defaults, and the `AttestConfig` type describes what `setup` accepts. `setup` analyzes only files under the working directory.

### skipTypes

`skipTypes` makes `setup` skip type-checking your project and skips every assertion that needs type information. Use it to iterate quickly when you're only changing runtime code.

You likely want two scripts:

```json
"test": "ATTEST_skipTypes=true vitest run",
"testWithTypes": "vitest run"
```

Use `test` when:

- You're only changing runtime logic
- You're running tests in watch mode or from your editor's test explorer

Use `testWithTypes` when:

- You've changed types and want to recheck your type-level assertions
- You're running tests in CI

### onlyNamedTestFiles

With `onlyNamedTestFiles`, `setup` type-checks only the test files named on the command line, e.g. `vitest run src/user.test.ts`. One file checks in seconds where a large project takes minutes. With no test file named, it checks every file as before.

A named file has to be a path to a file that exists, ends in `.test.ts` (or `.test.js`, `.test.mts`, `.test.tsx` and the like), and is part of your tsconfig. A test in a file that wasn't checked fails with "Found no assertion data", so a missed file can't pass silently.

Your runner must also run only the named files. Mocha runs files named on the command line in addition to the `spec` in its config, so leave the config out (`--no-package` if it's in `package.json`) and pass the options you need as flags. Vitest rejects flags it doesn't know, so set the environment variable instead:

```bash
ATTEST_onlyNamedTestFiles=true vitest run src/user.test.ts
```

### checker

The type checker attest analyzes type assertions with:

- `"tsjs"`: TypeScript's JS API, for TypeScript 6 and earlier
- `"tsgo"`: TypeScript 7's native compiler
- `"tsrs"`: [tsrs](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs), a faster Rust port of TypeScript 7 that serves the same API

By default, attest uses tsrs if it's installed alongside TypeScript 7 on a platform it ships a binary for, otherwise the checker matching your TypeScript version. Setting a checker that doesn't match your installed TypeScript throws.

### typeToStringFormat

[Prettier options](https://prettier.io/docs/en/options.html) for the type strings of `.type.toString` and `.jsdoc`. Yours override these defaults:

```json
{
	"semi": false,
	// note this print width is optimized for type serialization, not general code
	"printWidth": 60,
	"trailingComma": "none",
	"parser": "typescript"
}
```

As a flag or environment variable, pass them as JSON, e.g. `--typeToStringFormat '{ "useTabs": true }'`.

# CLI

> Summarize, trace and precache your project's type performance from the attest command.

`@ark/attest` installs an `attest` command, which you can run with `npx attest` or from a `package.json` script. `stats` and `trace` run `tsc` through `npm exec`, and both work for projects with `composite: true`.

## stats

```bash
npx attest stats packages/*
```

Type-checks each directory you pass with its own tsconfig, then prints its check time, type count and instantiation count, and the totals across all of them. With no arguments, it checks the current directory.

attest doesn't expand globs itself, so `packages/*` relies on your shell. Shells like Windows `cmd` don't expand it.

## trace

```bash
npx attest trace
```

Runs `tsc --generateTrace` on the `tsconfig.json` in the current directory and writes the results to `.attest/trace`:

- `trace.json`, which you can open in [Perfetto](https://ui.perfetto.dev/) as a type performance heat map
- `summary.txt`, with the slowest individual calls and the functions ranked by self time, which it also prints
- `ranges.csv` and `names.csv`, the same data per call and per function name

It has to run from a directory with a `tsconfig.json`. An optional argument sets the directory `tsc` runs in, which defaults to the current one.

## precache

```bash
npx attest precache
```

Writes the type data `setup` would, to `.attest/assertions.json` or the path you pass. Assertions read it from `.attest/assertions.json`, but `setup` deletes and rewrites that file, so a precached file is only used by tests that run without `setup`, e.g. CI jobs that share the output of one type-checking step.

# Custom assertions

> Read the type data attest collects from your own assertion functions.

If you're a library author who wants type data in your own assertions rather than through `attest`, tell `setup` which function names to analyze with `attestAliases`.

## Setup

```ts
import { setup } from "@ark/attest"

// replaces the default ["attest", "attestInternal"], so keep "attest" if you use it
setup({ attestAliases: ["attest", "yourCustomAssert"] })
```

`setup` has to run with these aliases before the first test. It finds every call to them in your project and writes their types to `.attest/assertions.json`, so assertions in any test process can read them without starting TypeScript.

## Type data

`caller` returns the position your function was called from, and `getTypeAssertionAtPosition` returns the data `setup` recorded for the call there:

```ts
import { caller, getTypeAssertionAtPosition } from "@ark/attest"

export const yourCustomAssert = <expectedType>(actualValue: expectedType) => {
	const assertion = getTypeAssertionAtPosition(caller())
	const actual = assertion.args[0]
	// how the value's type relates to the expected type argument
	const relationship = actual.relationships.typeArgs[0]
	if (relationship === undefined) {
		throw new Error(
			`yourCustomAssert requires an expected type, e.g. yourCustomAssert<"foo">("foo")`
		)
	}
	if (relationship !== "equality") {
		throw new Error(
			`Expected ${assertion.typeArgs[0].type}, got ${actual.type} with relationship ${relationship}`
		)
	}
}
```

A user might then call it like this:

```ts
import { yourCustomAssert } from "your-package"

// passes
yourCustomAssert<"foo">(`${"f"}oo` as const)
// throws "Expected boolean, got true with relationship subtype"
yourCustomAssert<boolean>(true)
// throws "Expected 5, got number with relationship supertype"
// @ts-expect-error
yourCustomAssert<5>(2 + 3)
```

The data for each call (`TypeAssertionData`) has:

- `args` and `typeArgs`: for each argument and type argument, its `type` as TypeScript displays it, and `relationships.args` and `relationships.typeArgs`, how it relates to each argument and type argument: `"subtype"`, `"supertype"`, `"equality"` or `"none"`
- `errors`: the messages of the type errors reported for the call
- `completions`: the completions of each string literal in the first argument
- `jsdoc`: the JSDoc of the first argument, if any
- `location`: the call's start and end `{ line, char }`

If your assertion is called through a helper of yours, `caller()` returns the position of the call in the helper. Pass `caller({ upStackBy: 4 })` to look one call further up the stack, or a `skip` function that returns `true` for each position to move past, e.g. `caller({ skip: position => position.method === "yourHelper" })`.

## Instantiations

A call to `.instantiations` on an alias, e.g. `yourCustomAssert.instantiations()`, records the instantiations contributed by the test it's in. `getBenchAssertionAtPosition` returns that count:

```ts
import { caller, getBenchAssertionAtPosition } from "@ark/attest"

yourCustomAssert.instantiations = (max: number) => {
	const { count } = getBenchAssertionAtPosition(caller())
	if (count > max) throw new Error(`${count} instantiations exceeds ${max}`)
}
```

## Without setup

`writeAssertionData(path)` type-checks your project and writes the type data to `path`, as `setup` does without deleting `.attest` or recording config. Assertions read it from `.attest/assertions.json`.

For questions or feedback, open an [issue](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/issues/new/choose) or [discussion](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/discussions/new/choose) on GitHub, or ask on [ArkType's Discord](https://arktype.io/discord).
